For microbial communities analysis, DNA was extracted from the biofilm on plastic and gravel 23 substrates, and then the 16S rRNA was sequenced through the Illumina Miseq platform. 24 Cultivation was performed to isolate strains from the plastic and gravel substrates. Substrate type 25 strongly influenced the microbial composition and structure, while no difference between sites was 26 detected. Although several taxa were shared among plastics, we observed some groups specific for 27 each plastic substrate. These communities comprised taxa previously reported from both epipelagic 28 zones and deep-sea benthic ecosystems. The core microbiome (microbial taxa shared by all plastic 29 substrates) was exclusively composed by low abundance taxa, with some members well-described 30 in the plastisphere and with known plastic-degradation capabilities. Additionally, we obtained 31 bacterial strains that have been previously reported inhabiting plastic substrates and/or degrading 32 hydrocarbon compounds, which corroborates our metabarcoding data and suggests the presence of 33 microbial members potentially active and involved with degradation of these plastics in the deep 34 sea.

In summary, this study reported for the first time that deep-sea microbial communities of the 537 Southwest Atlantic Ocean are involved in the colonization of plastic substrates. Furthermore, the 538 microbial community colonizing the plastic surfaces were distinct and dependent on polymer type, 539 but the site where the samples were deployed had no effect on the microbial community. Our 540 results demonstrated a core microbiome exclusively composed of low abundance taxa; some 541 members were not previously described as associated with plastic substrates, while other bacterial 542 families had previously been described degrading plastics, but not in deep-sea environments.

Additionally, we were able to cultivate and isolate some of these bacterial families from our plastic 544 substrates. Our results indicate that a specific microbial community from the deep-sea can attach, 545 colonize and potentially degrade plastic substrates. As a 40 consequence, marine plastic contamination is ubiquitous, including in remote marine environments 41 such as the deep ocean (Woodal et. al., 2014). In the marine environment, plastic waste is exposed 42 to physical and chemical factors that contribute to the degradation and fragmentation of this 43 material into microplastics (i.e. plastic objects < 5 mm in diameter) (Roager and Sonnenschein, 44 2019) . Microplastic chemical composition, density and shape determine whether it is more likely 45 to float or sink, which will influence the distribution in pelagic or benthic ecosystems (Cole et al., 46 2011; Pierdomenico et al., 2019; Pinnell and Turner, 2019; Van Cauwenberghe et al., 2013; 47 Woodall et al., 2014) . Although both macroand microplastics have already been reported in deep-48 ocean regions, knowledge regarding plastic colonization by deep-sea prokaryotic communities in 49 both pelagic and benthic ecosystems is incipient (Bergmann and Klages, 2012; Chiba et al., 2018; 50 Galgani et al., 1996; Krause et al., 2020; Pierdomenico et al., 2019; Schlining et al., 2013; Woodall 51 et al., 2018).

Plastic substrates in the deep ocean may offer a new hotspot of 57 colonization, as well as a relevant source of carbon to support the microbial community, 58 proportionally magnifying the abundance of potentially plastic degrading microorganisms within 59 4 the plastisphere. A growing number of studies have reported microorganisms capable of degrading 60 hydrocarbons (Didier et al., 2017; Oberbeckmann et al., 2017), raising the hypothesis that they 61 would be consuming this material in nutritionally limited conditions, such as those found in deep-62 sea ecosystems. 63 In addition to the influence of the environment (which can be prone to microbial colonization or 64 not), polymer composition is suggested to modulate the structure and composition of the 65 plastisphere (Dussud et al., 2018a; Dussud et al., 2018b; Kirstein et al., 2018, 2019; McCormick 66 et al., 2014; Pinto et al., 2019; Zettler et al., 2013). Moreover, geographic locations have also been 67 indicated to exert influence on the microbial community of the plastisphere (Oberbeckmann et al., 68 2016). In contrast, independent of environmental factors or plastic substrate type, some microbial 69 taxa have been reported in multiple plastispheres (Tu et al., 2020; Zettler et al., 2013) and they are 70 now referred to as "core microbiome". The core microbiome members comprise taxa with high 71 occupancy across a dataset that are hypothesized to reflect functional relationships with the host 72 (or substrate) (Shade and Handelsman, 2012). In the plastisphere, these members are thought to be 73 involved in biofilm formation and/or metabolizing compounds from the plastic substrate (Didier 74 et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2020). Bacterial families such as Oleiphilaceae and Hyphomonadaceae have 75 been found colonizing multiple substrates (Bryant et al., 2016; De Tender et al., 2017; 76 Oberbeckmann et al., 2018; Pinto et al., 2019; Zettler et al., 2013). The known capacity of these 77 families to metabolize hydrocarbon compounds may be the key functional trait enabling them to 78 colonize different plastics (Golyshin et al., 2002; Ozaki et al., 2007).

Together with 347 a general reduction of organic matter input, these extreme conditions promote high selective 348 pressures on the microbial community. The input of anthropogenic substrates (i.e., sources of 349 carbon) into the deep sea, such as plastic substrates, creates new habitats (or food sources) to be 350 colonized by microorganisms. However, the composition of these substrata may select pelagic 351 microorganisms with specific features that allow them to colonize and metabolize this carbon352 source (Dussud et al., 2018a; Dussud et al., 2018b). 353 Although the input of organic matter is suggested to be low, the pool of organic matter in deep 354 waters could be enough to support high microbial richness (Luna et al., 2012), as indicated by our 355 results. The highest richness on the gravel samples indicates that more microbial taxa were capable 356 of attaching to the gravel in comparison with the plastic substrates, suggesting that plastics likely 357 offer a strong selective pressure to colonization by the surrounding microbial community 358 (McCormick et al., 2014). This is also supported by the lower microbial evenness observed in the 359 plastic substrates (Figure S1C). However, statistical differences in alpha-diversity indices between 360 plastic substrates and AW were not observed. Despite the high variability among samples and a 361 limited number of replicates, these results indicate that the substrate effect on microbial 362 communities is reflected by taxonomic composition rather than by diversity indexes. To the best 363 of our knowledge, there is no previous study that has experimentally addressed the microbial 364 colonization on plastic substrates in deep waters. Several previous studies have reported on surface 365 waters (either from laboratory or field experiments) a lower richness and diversity of plastic 366 substrates in comparison with the surrounding waters, suggesting that plastic substrates select for 367 a specific and less diverse microbial community (McCormick et al., 2014; Ogonowski et al., 2018; 368 Zettler et al., 2013). Nevertheless, deep water is generally oligotrophic, while surface waters have 369 a constant input of organic matter from primary production from the phytoplanktonic community 370

The AW samples are therefore a type of control, providing 404 information on the microbial taxa present in the water column before retrieving the substrates. 405 Corroborating our results, Oberbeckmann et al., (2016) demonstrated significant differences of 406 multiple taxonomic groups when comparing plastic biofilm communities and the surrounding 407 seawater communities; although the bacterial communities attached to PET bottles were distinct 408from the free-living seawater communities, the authors also found that PET-associated 409 communities were similar to other types of particle-associated or glass-bound communities 410 collected in the surrounding seawater. Additionally, bacterial families classified as Flavobacteriaceae, Pirellulaceae, 421 Rhodobacteraceae (Alphaproteobacteria) and Microtrichaceae (Acidimicrobiia) were identified as 422 the most dominant families on microplastic (PE) biofilms exposed for 135 days to the marine 423 environment at 12 m depth (Tu et al., 2020).424 When comparing our microbial taxa from plastic substrates with previous studies related to the 425 plastisphere in epipelagic ecosystems we found several families in common, Oleiphilaceae and Bacillaceae (Amaral-Zettler et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020; 429 Pinto et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020). The family Oleiphilaceae comprises members that 430 obligately utilize hydrocarbons through the alkane hydroxylase (AlkB) pathway (Golyshin et al., 431 2002); its detection in our plastic samples likely indicates their potential role in degrading plastic 432 substrates in deep-sea ecosystems. Further, among the families described by these authors, 433 Rhodospirillaceae members were not detected in our samples, which is in agreement with their 434 photosynthetic capacity and thus their prevalence in epipelagic ecosystems. We detected a few 435 22 families in our plastic samples which were not identified in these previous studies, such as 436 Nitrosopumilaceae. Nitrosopumilaceae members are widely distributed in several deep-sea 437 environments and have an important role as primary producers through ammonia oxidation (Zhong 438 et al., 2020). Their presence in our plastic substrates likely reflects the high abundance of this 439 family in these ecosystems, which might favor their attachment to a variety of substrates available 440 for colonization. 441 Remarkable differences were observed when we grouped the microbial families by their 442 distributions amongst plastic types as generalists (significantly abundant on all plastic types, 443 HDPE, HDPE-OXO and PP), HDPE plastic generalists (significantly abundant in HDPE and 444 HDPE-OXO), and specialists (significantly abundant in specific plastic substrates). Members of 445 Bdellovibrionaceae, Halieaceae, Microtrichaceae and Pseudomonadaceae families were identified 446 as generalists. The ability to colonize and potentially metabolize the carbon from plastic polymers 447 of different substrates in deep environments, under oligotrophic conditions, confer advantages on 448 these microbes in comparison to the entire microbial community. Some of these families have been 449 previously described in association with different types of microplastics from several locations 450 (e.g. Dussud et al., 2018a; Jiang et al., 2018; Tu et al., 2020). Tu et al., (2020) found a high 451 abundance of Microtrichaceae members within biofilms of polyethylene microplastics from coastal 452 seawater in the Yellow Sea, China, with increasing abundance according to longer exposure 453 periods (135 days). Halieaceae members were detected in polyethylene, polypropylene and 454 polystyrene microplastics from the Yangtze estuary (Jiang et al., 2018) and polyethylene 455 microplastics from the Yellow Sea (Tu et al., 2020), both in China. This family is composed by 456 marine bacteria that are capable of assimilating propylene through alkene monooxygenase genes 457 (Suzuki et al., 2019). In addition, we observed microbial families associated specifically to HDPE 458 23 samples (with and without biodegradable additives). Those microbes, in contrast to the generalist 459 group, are suggested to be more adaptive to colonizing HDPE polymers, with weak or no influence 460 from biodegradable additives. The influence of biodegradable additives was observed in the 461 specialist taxa group (i.e. those microbes more adapted to a specific polymer type). The presence 462 of additives in the polymer compositions may support microbial dynamics over time (Dussud et 463 al., 2018b). Additionally, those additives could be an extra source of nutrients that may reflect in 464 the multiplication of the different microorganisms. Similar results were reported by Dussud et al., 465 (2018b) that suggested a strong effect of the polymer type on the bacterial community, because the 466 composition of microbial biofilm on LDPE and LDPE-OXO (PE with pro-oxidant additives) was 467 completely distinct, while AA-LDPE-OXO (artificially aged LDPE-OXO) and PHBV (poly(3-468 hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) showed higher similarity, all under controlled conditions. 469 As observed by these authors for shallow waters, we also observed an influence of the plastic types 470 HDPE and HDPE-OXO on selecting specific microbial taxa in deep waters. 471 A total of 28 ASVs were identified as core microbiome members in the plastisphere. Defining a 472 common core microbiome in the plastisphere across different studies may be difficult, because 473 variations between experimental designs make it difficult to compare studies directly, as do the 474 variety of study-specific approaches used to define the core (Didier et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2020; 475 Zettler et al., 2013). However, some taxa observed in our study were widely described by previous 476 studies, which provides evidence of common core members of the plastisphere from both surface 477 and deep waters. ASVs from the bacterial families Oleiphilaceae and Hyphomonadaceae were 478 found as members of the core microbiome in our plastic samples. These families have members 479 known to degrade hydrocarbons (Golyshin et al., 2002; Ozaki et al., 2007) or are frequently 480 24 associated to plastic substrates in the marine environment (Bryant et al., 2016; De Tender et al., 481 2017; Oberbeckmann et al., 2018; Pinto et al., 2019; Zettler et al., 2013). 482 In addition, taxa reported from plastic substrates, but not in the core microbiome were also 483 identified. Notably, taxa not 486 previously described from plastic substrates were also identified. Micrococcaceae is a well-487 documented bacterial family inhabiting deep-sea sediments (Chen et al., 2005, 2016; Sass et al., 488 2001); their members were already identified in sediments from the Southwest Indian Ridge at 489 depths ranging from 1,662 to 4,000 m (Chen et al., 2016), in a hypersaline 3,500 m depth site in 490 the Mediterranean Sea (Sass et al., 2001), and were isolated from an Antarctic lake and deep-sea 491 sediments from the tropical West Pacific (Chen et al., 2005). Studies that assessed marine plastisphere microbial communities can be classified into three basic groups: those that randomly collected plastic marine debris (PMD) or microplastics (Bryant et al., 2016; De Tender et al., 2015; Zettler et al., 2013); studies that deployed plastic substrates in the ocean (Oberbeckmann et al., 2016; Tu et al., 2020) and those conducted in laboratory conditions (Kirstein et al., 2018; Ogonowski et al., 2018). The microbial community structure inhabiting deployed plastic substrates for long periods is as yet poorly studied (Kirstein et al., 2018; Oberbeckmann et al., 2016, 2018; Tu et al., 2020). Based on these studies, the marine plastic bacterial community is mainly represented by the Gammaproteobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria and Bacteroidetes classes, while the archaeal community is represented by 92 the Euryarchaeota and Crenarchaeota phyla (Eriksen et al., 2014; Oberbeckmann et al., 2018; Oberbeckmann and Labrenz, 2020; Quero and Luna, 2017; Urbanek et al., 2018; Woodall et al., 2018) . Here, we conducted the first in situ experimental study that characterized the structure and composition of the microbial community (the bacterial and archaeal) associated with different types of plastic substrates deployed for 719 days at three sites in deep waters in the Southwest 98 (SW) Atlantic Ocean (3,300 m).
